blocks.text: Sending one request, waiting for its response, then sending the next, works fine most of the time, but when a client needs several independent pieces of information at once, that back and forth adds up. Batching lets several requests travel together in a single message, and their responses come back together too, trimming away unnecessary round trips.
1. What Batching Actually Solves

blocks.alt: Request 1 and request 2 combine into one batch

blocks.text: Every request-response round trip carries some fixed overhead, network latency, connection handling, serialization, when a client needs to make several independent calls, sending them one at a time pays that overhead repeatedly, batching pays it once for the whole group instead.

blocks.title: A useful analogy
blocks.content: Batching is a lot like combining several errands into one trip instead of driving back and forth separately for each one.

blocks.text: This overhead becomes especially noticeable for a remote server, covered in the Transport Mechanisms module, where every round trip crosses a real network rather than staying within one machine.
Even a small fixed cost per round trip multiplies quickly once dozens of independent calls are involved.
Batching exists specifically to reclaim that repeated cost.
2. The Shape of a Batch Message

blocks.alt: An array of requests is sent as one message

blocks.text: A batch is simply a JSON array containing several individual request objects, each with its own id, method, and params, exactly as if they had been sent separately, just grouped together in one array.
Each item inside the array is a complete, valid request on its own, batching does not change the shape of an individual request, only how many are sent together.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Nothing about an individual request changes when it is placed inside a batch, the same method and params it would have used standalone.

blocks.text: 3. The Shape of a Batch Response

The server replies with a matching array of responses, one per request in the batch, each still carrying its own id so the client can match every response back to the exact request it answers, exactly the same id-matching logic used for individual requests.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Meaning"],"rows":[["id","Matches back to the original request"],["result or error","The outcome of that specific request"]]}

blocks.text: Nothing about how a single response is interpreted changes just because it arrived as part of an array.
4. Batch Responses Are Not Necessarily in Order

Even within a batch response array, the server is not required to return results in the exact same order the requests appeared, this is exactly why id-based matching, rather than positional matching, remains essential even for batched calls.
A server might process a slow request last even though it appeared first in the batch, or process several concurrently and return whichever finishes first, order is never guaranteed.
A server processing requests concurrently internally has no reason to wait and preserve input order when writing out its response array.
5. Batching Is Optional, Not Universal

Not every MCP client or server implementation supports batching, it is treated as an optional capability rather than a mandatory part of the protocol, a client should check for batching support before relying on it, falling back to individual requests otherwise.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Capability check","Meaning"],"rows":[["batching present","Server accepts arrays of requests"],["batching absent","Client must send requests individually"]]}

blocks.text: Checking this once during initialization is enough, the answer stays fixed for the rest of that session.
6. When Batching Genuinely Helps

blocks.alt: Many small requests benefit from batching, which reduces round trips

blocks.text: Batching pays off most clearly when a client already knows, upfront, that it needs several independent pieces of information, discovering a server tools, resources, and prompts all at once during initialization is a natural, common example.
Another common case is a dashboard-style application that needs several independent pieces of status information refreshed at once, batching keeps that refresh to a single round trip.

blocks.title: A concrete trigger
blocks.content: Ask whether the client already knows every piece of information it needs before making the first call, if so, batching is worth considering.

blocks.text: This is exactly the scenario the initialization discovery step benefits from most.
7. When Batching Does Not Help

If one request genuinely depends on the result of another, reading a resource whose URI comes from an earlier tool call, batching does not help, those calls have to happen sequentially regardless, since the second one cannot be constructed until the first result is known.

blocks.title: A quick test
blocks.content: Ask whether request two could be constructed without knowing the result of request one, if not, batching them together is not possible.

blocks.text: Sequential dependencies like this are common whenever one call discovers something the next call needs to act on.
Recognizing this upfront saves time spent trying to force independence onto calls that genuinely have none.
8. A Partial Failure Inside a Batch

blocks.alt: A batch of 3 can have one request fail

blocks.text: One request inside a batch can fail while the others succeed, the batch response simply contains a mix of successful results and error objects, one per original request, a client needs to check each individual response rather than assuming the whole batch succeeded or failed together.
This partial-failure behavior mirrors how a promise all with individual error handling works in many programming languages, some succeed, some fail, independently.
A client that assumes all-or-nothing success will misinterpret a batch where only some calls actually failed.
9. Constructing a Batch on the Client Side
A client typically builds the batch by assembling a list of individual request objects, each with a freshly generated id, then sending the whole array as one transport-level message.
Most MCP client SDKs that support batching provide a dedicated helper method specifically for this, sparing a developer from assembling the raw array by hand.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["1","Assemble a list of independent requests"],["2","Assign each a unique id"],["3","Send the whole array as one message"]]}

blocks.text: This helper usually also handles distributing each response back to its correct pending caller automatically.
10. Batching vs Parallel Individual Requests

blocks.alt: A batch takes one trip while parallel requests take multiple trips

blocks.text: Sending several individual requests without waiting for each response, covered in the Requests lesson, achieves a similar concurrency benefit without needing explicit batch support, batching additionally saves the transport-level overhead of separate messages, but the two approaches often overlap in practice.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Requires batch support","Saves transport overhead"],"rows":[["Batching","Yes","Yes"],["Concurrent individual requests","No","No, but still saves waiting time"]]}

blocks.text: In practice, many hosts simply send several individual requests without waiting between them, achieving most of batching practical benefit without needing the server to support the batch capability at all.

code.content:
# concurrent individual requests, no batch capability needed
results = await asyncio.gather(
    client.send_request("tools/list"),
    client.send_request("resources/list"),
)

blocks.text: 11. Batching and Session Initialization

The initialize request itself is never batched with anything else, since nothing else can safely be sent before the handshake completes, batching only becomes relevant for requests sent after a session is already active.
This restriction exists precisely because capabilities, negotiated during initialize, are what determine whether batching itself is even available for anything sent afterward.
12. Batching Notifications Alongside Requests

A batch can mix requests and notifications together in the same array, the server processes each item according to its own type, sending a response only for the items that were actual requests, notifications inside the batch still receive no reply, exactly as they would if sent individually.
13. Deciding How Large a Batch Should Be

blocks.alt: A small batch is compared against a large batch

blocks.text: A very large batch can itself become a problem, tying up server resources processing dozens of requests at once, most practical implementations keep batches modest in size, grouping only the handful of genuinely independent calls a specific moment actually needs.

code.content:
# a simple cap on batch size
MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 10
batch = requests[:MAX_BATCH_SIZE]

blocks.text: A reasonable starting point is grouping only what one specific screen or task genuinely needs at once.
14. A Worked Example
Trace a client batching a discovery step, listing tools, resources, and prompts together in one round trip.

code.content:
responses = client.send_batch([
    {"method": "tools/list"},
    {"method": "resources/list"},
    {"method": "prompts/list"},
])
for r in responses:
    print(r["id"], "->", r.get("result", r.get("error")))

blocks.text: Notice that even though these three calls have no dependency on each other, the client still needs three separate ids to correctly match each result back to its originating request.
This same three-call pattern is exactly what a client typically performs once, right after a session becomes active.
15. Common Mistakes When Using Batching

items: Assuming batch responses arrive in the same order the requests were sent, they do not, id matching is still required.
Batching requests that actually depend on each other sequentially, when they cannot be resolved together at all.
Assuming a whole batch fails if one request inside it fails, individual results within a batch are independent.
Using batching without first confirming the server actually supports it as a capability.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is sending an enormous batch of unrelated requests purely to minimize round trips, without considering the burst load this places on the server all at once.
A sixth common mistake is forgetting to give every request inside a batch its own unique id, causing responses to be matched incorrectly.
Duplicate ids inside one batch are just as problematic as duplicate ids across separate individual requests.
16. Practice: Batch Your Own Discovery Step

Write out the exact batch request array you would send to discover all three of a server tools, resources, and prompts in one round trip, and the batch response array you would expect back if all three succeeded.
As a further exercise, sketch what the batch response would look like if the prompts/list request specifically failed while the other two succeeded.
Compare the two response shapes side by side to see exactly where the difference lives.
Key Takeaway

Batching groups several independent requests into one message, and their responses come back together too, still matched individually by id, saving round trips when a client already knows it needs several unrelated pieces of information at once, though it remains an optional capability and does not help when calls genuinely depend on each other.

This lesson builds on the Requests and Responses lessons from the MCP Fundamentals module, and connects forward to Streaming next, which covers responses that arrive incrementally rather than all at once, a different way of handling operations that take real time.

The mixed batch concept from the newly added section is worth remembering, a batch is not limited to only requests, it can include notifications too, each handled according to its own type within the same single transport-level message.
